995.title: Forgiveness Sunday
995.hook: before Lent, Orthodox Christians ask forgiveness of one another
995.howItsDone: On the Sunday before Great Lent, Orthodox Christians end the evening service with a rite of mutual forgiveness: each person bows to the others, asks forgiveness, and receives it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kshamavani, the Jain day, and two words sent wide: micchami dukkadam. Today, another day of forgiveness, this time in a church, face to face.

The evening service is ending, but nobody leaves. Instead, the people form a line. The priest stands at the front, and one by one the congregation comes to him, and then to each other. Each person stops in front of the next, bows, and says two words; then the other bows back. The grandmother and the teenager. The choir director and the man who complained about the choir. Neighbors who haven't spoken since an argument over a fence. This is the Sunday before Lent in the Orthodox churches, and the Christians who keep it call it Forgiveness Sunday.
screen: `NOBODY LEAVES.` → `A LINE, AND A BOW.` → `THE SUNDAY BEFORE LENT.`

segments.voice: First, the two words. In English, they're forgive me. The answer, in some parishes, is something like: God forgives, and I forgive. The wording varies from place to place, but the shape stays: each person asks first. Second, why asking comes first. It would be easy to walk down the line saying I forgive you, I forgive you, as if everyone else were the problem. The rite turns that around. Everyone asks, the person who was wronged too. In a line like that, nobody gets to be only the injured party. Third, the Gospel behind it. By tradition, the reading for this Sunday comes from Matthew, including the words: "For if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you". Then the passage turns to fasting: "Moreover when ye fast, be not, as the hypocrites, of a sad countenance". Forgiveness first, then the fast. Fourth, why before Lent. Lent is a long season of fasting and prayer, and Orthodox Christians begin it the next day. In this rite, peace with the people around you comes before the long fast. This path met the same order a few weeks back, in the gift left waiting at the altar. First the person in front of you. Then Lent begins.
screen: `FORGIVE ME. GOD FORGIVES.` · `EVERYONE ASKS FIRST.` · `IF YE FORGIVE MEN.` · `PEACE FIRST, THEN THE FAST.` · then, large: `FORGIVE ME.`

segments.voice: Picture a line of people you know, family, friends, coworkers, standing quietly, and walk down it slowly in your mind. At each face, don't decide who was right; just notice whether there's anything, even small, you'd ask forgiveness for, and when you find one, let the line stop. Let the two words form silently, forgive me, and notice how they sit in the mouth; if you pray, you can bring that person and the words into your prayer.
Forgiveness Sunday. The Orthodox Christian day before Lent when people ask forgiveness of one another, face to face. Today's word.
Your line: forgive me. In that line everyone asks, even the one who was wronged. Until tomorrow.

996.title: Laylat al-Qadr
996.hook: in Ramadan's last nights, Muslims pray for forgiveness on the Night of Power (Quran 97)
996.howItsDone: Muslims seek Laylat al-Qadr in the last nights of Ramadan with extra prayer, Qur'an recitation and supplication, and the supplication the Prophet taught Aisha, asking God to pardon, is said on those nights.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Forgiveness Sunday, a line of bows before Lent. Your line was forgive me. Today, the last of these days of forgiveness: a single night, hidden somewhere near the end of Ramadan.

It's past midnight near the end of Ramadan, and the mosque is still lit. Some people stand in prayer. Some sit against the wall with the Qur'an open on their knees. Some have brought blankets and will stay until dawn. At home, others pray quietly in a back room while the house sleeps. Nobody knows for certain which of these nights is the one they're looking for. That's part of it. The night has a name, and a whole short chapter of the Qur'an to itself. Laylat al-Qadr: the Night of Power.
screen: `PAST MIDNIGHT, STILL LIT.` → `WHICH NIGHT IS IT?` → `THE NIGHT OF POWER.`

segments.voice: First, what the Qur'an says. Surah ninety-seven is short. In Pickthall's translation it opens: "Lo! We revealed it on the Night of Power." Muslims understand it to be the Qur'an, first sent down on this night. Then a startling comparison: "The Night of Power is better than a thousand months." Second, how it ends. The angels and the Spirit come down, the chapter says, and the night is "Peace until the rising of the dawn." Not a night of fear or judgment: a night of peace. Third, the hiding. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, told his followers to seek the night in the last nights of Ramadan, the odd-numbered ones, according to a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari. That hadith gives no single date, so people keep watch across several nights. Some readers see the hiding as a mercy of its own: it keeps people praying longer. Fourth, the question his wife asked. In a hadith recorded by al-Tirmidhi, Aisha asks him what she should say if she knows which night it is. He teaches her a short supplication, in paraphrase: God, you are the one who pardons, and you love to pardon, so pardon me. Of all the things to ask for on a night better than a thousand months, the answer he gives is forgiveness.
screen: `WE REVEALED IT ON THIS NIGHT.` · `BETTER THAN A THOUSAND MONTHS.` · `PEACE UNTIL THE DAWN.` · `YOU LOVE TO PARDON, SO PARDON ME.` · then, large: `THE NIGHT OF POWER.`

segments.voice: Let these minutes be a small night watch, whatever the hour, and bring to mind the first thing you'd ask to be forgiven for, without explaining or defending it. Then, in your own way, ask: if you pray, with the words of your own tradition, or, if you're Muslim, the words the Prophet taught Aisha. If you don't pray, simply let yourself want it to be let go, and stay with that wanting.
Laylat al-Qadr. The Night of Power, in the last nights of Ramadan, when the Qur'an was first revealed and Muslims keep watch and ask forgiveness. Today's word.
Your line: the night of power. A night of peace, until the dawn. That's day nine hundred ninety-six.

997.title: Different answers
997.hook: teshuvah, grace, mercy, karma's release, reciprocity: forgiveness means different things in each home
997.carry: kept whole, in its own words
997.howItsDone: On this path, people study each tradition's teaching on forgiveness in its own words, and some keep a journal where they write what forgiveness means to them.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Laylat al-Qadr, the Night of Power in Ramadan's last nights. Your line was the night of power.

Five cards on a kitchen table, face up. Teshuvah. Grace. Mercy. Release. Reciprocity. Flip any one over, and the back reads the same English word: forgiveness. For weeks, this block has visited homes that each keep that word in a different room. Tomorrow the question closes. Today the cards go side by side: not to choose a winner, not to blend them into one, just to see each clearly, in its own home. Different answers to the same human need.
screen: `FIVE CARDS, ONE WORD ON THE BACK.` → `EACH IN ITS OWN HOME.`

segments.voice: First, teshuvah, a Hebrew word that means return. The Jewish teacher Maimonides lays it out as a path: leave the wrong, regret it, resolve not to go back to it, and confess it. For wrongs against people, Jewish teaching adds making it right with the person hurt. Forgiveness here is a road someone walks back along. Second, grace, a Christian word. Christian teaching speaks of forgiveness as a gift from God that no one earns, and of passing that gift on. The Lord's Prayer puts the two side by side, in the King James words: "And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors." Third, mercy. The Qur'an tells people who have wronged themselves not to despair of God's mercy, and calls God the Forgiving, the Merciful. Fourth, two more answers, from the East. The first is release. In Jain teaching, holding on to anger binds karma to the soul, and asking and giving forgiveness loosens it. The Buddhist Dhammapada points the same way: hatred never ends by hatred, only by its opposite. The second is reciprocity. Confucius is asked for one word to live by. His answer, in Legge's translation: "What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others." Some of these overlap. Some don't. Each tradition would want its answer kept whole, in its own words, not stirred into the others. The point isn't which one is right. It's that forgiveness has been thought about with great care, in many homes, and there's more than one way in.
screen: `TESHUVAH — THE ROAD BACK.` · `GRACE — A GIFT PASSED ON.` · `MERCY — DO NOT DESPAIR.` · `RELEASE AND RECIPROCITY.` · then, large: `DIFFERENT ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: Read the five words to yourself, slowly: return, gift, mercy, release, reciprocity, and notice which one stays with you, without deciding why. Then write one sentence, on paper or your phone, that begins: forgiveness, to me, is. Let it be your own words, not the right words; if you pray, you can hold the sentence in your prayer.
Different answers. Return, grace, mercy, release and reciprocity: the shapes forgiveness takes in different homes, each kept whole. Today's word.
Your line: kept whole, in its own words. Five homes, five answers, none of them stirred into the others. Day nine hundred ninety-seven, done.

998.title: Forgiveness close
998.hook: sixty days on the hardest gift
998.howItsDone: Some traditions mark forgiveness with a gesture of release, such as casting crumbs into water at Tashlich, asking forgiveness aloud at Kshamavani, or a bedtime prayer that forgives the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was different answers: return, grace, mercy, release, reciprocity. Your line was kept whole, in its own words.

A brother runs down a road toward the twin who cheated him. Genesis says it plainly, in the King James words: "And Esau ran to meet him, and embraced him, and fell on his neck, and kissed him: and they wept." That was early in this block. Since then: a guard who reached out his hand, a bedtime prayer, a Jain phrase sent wide, a day of fasting, and a long list of people who are hard to forgive. Sixty days on what this path called the hardest gift. Today it all gathers up, and then comes the one thing the whole block has been circling: let one thing go.
screen: `ESAU RUNS.` → `SIXTY DAYS ON THE HARDEST GIFT.` → `LET ONE THING GO.`

segments.voice: First, what forgiveness isn't. Forgiving is not excusing: the wrong stays named as a wrong. It isn't the same as reconciling, which takes two people and happens only where it's safe. And not yet is allowed. Second, the order. A Jewish teaching said that for wrongs between people, you go to the person first. Jesus told the one bringing a gift to leave it at the altar and be reconciled first. A good apology owns the wrong and repairs it. Third, the stories. Joseph wept aloud before his brothers. Esau ran. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, at Ta'if, did not curse the town that drove him out. Angulimala stopped. Each is a picture of something held, and a hand that opens. Fourth, the times set aside: the Days of Awe and Yom Kippur, Kshamavani, Forgiveness Sunday, the Night of Power, the small nightly prayer before sleep, and yesterday's five answers, each in its own home. So what does let it go mean, after all that? Not that the thing was fine. Not forgetting, or going back. It means you stop carrying it everywhere you go. Paul's letter to the Colossians puts it in the King James words: "forbearing one another, and forgiving one another, if any man have a quarrel against any". A quarrel is real. And it can still be set down.
screen: `NOT EXCUSING. NOT ALWAYS RETURNING.` · `THE PERSON FIRST.` · `A HAND THAT OPENS.` · `THE TIMES SET ASIDE.` · then, large: `LET IT GO.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small thing you've been carrying, a comment, a slight, a grudge with no one left to argue with, and name it silently as what it was. Rest one hand palm up on your knee as if it sat there, and on each slow out-breath let the hand soften: not saying it was okay, just putting it down for now. If it comes back, notice it and set it down again; if you pray, you can offer it in your own way.
Quarrel. Paul's word in Colossians for the real complaint that forbearing and forgiving can still set down. Today's word.
Your line: let it go. Sixty days on the hardest gift, gathered into three words. Tomorrow, a new question: awe.

999.title: What awe is
999.hook: the feeling of something vast that you can't quite take in; every tradition names it differently
999.howItsDone: People on this path often mark awe by pausing outdoors, at the sea, on a mountain or under the night sky, and by reading the passages different traditions wrote about such moments.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was quarrel, a real complaint that can still be set down. Your line was let it go, and with it, sixty days on forgiveness closed.

The edge of a canyon, where the ground simply stops. A thunderstorm rolling in over a lake. A newborn's whole hand wrapped around one finger. A night sky so far from town that the stars look crowded. Some things don't fit. The mind tries to take them in and runs out of room. For some, the breath catches; for others, there's stillness, or a laugh, or tears that make no sense. Then the moment passes. For the weeks ahead, this path stays with that moment, starting with the plainest question: what is it?
screen: `THE EDGE OF A CANYON.` → `SOME THINGS DON'T FIT.` → `WHAT IS IT?`

segments.voice: First, an old word with two sides. Some readers hear the old word fear, in lines like this one, as something closer to awe. The psalm says, in the King James words: "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom". Not terror that makes you run. More like standing very still because you've met something larger than you. Second, a scholar's name for it. Rudolf Otto, a German writer on religion, described the holy as a mystery that makes people tremble and draws them in at the same time. He used Latin for it: mysterium tremendum, a mystery that makes one tremble, and fascinans, what draws one in. Terrible and fascinating at once. Third, the strange thing about awe: it's often about what was there all along. Emerson, in his essay Nature, tries a thought experiment: "If the stars should appear one night in a thousand years, how would men believe and adore; and preserve for many generations the remembrance of the city of God which had been shown!" And yet, he says, they come out every night, and we barely look. Fourth, the names. A psalm calls it glory. Moses is told he stands on holy ground. Jacob wakes and says he didn't know. The Qur'an calls such things signs. Each one gets its own day ahead, in its own words. Different words, one shared gesture underneath: looking up from what's in your hands to what's around you.
screen: `FEAR AND AWE, TWO SIDES.` · `TERRIBLE AND FASCINATING AT ONCE.` · `IT WAS THERE ALL ALONG.` · `MANY NAMES, ONE GESTURE.` · then, large: `LOOK UP.`

segments.voice: Lift your eyes slowly above everything you usually look at, screens, faces, tables, to the sky if you have it, or a treetop, or just the ceiling and the light coming in. For one minute, don't name what you see; let it be bigger than you, and let thoughts pass under it like birds. If you pray, the looking can be your prayer.
Mysterium tremendum. Rudolf Otto's Latin for the holy: a mystery that makes one tremble and draws one in at once. Today's word.
Your line: look up. The stars come out every night, whether anyone looks or not. One day short of a thousand.

1000.title: The heavens declare
1000.hook: the heavens declare the glory of God (Psalm 19:1)
1000.howItsDone: Psalm 19 is prayed in Jewish and Christian worship; some people on other paths read its first line outdoors, at sunrise or under the night sky.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was mysterium tremendum: awe, terrible and fascinating at once. Your line was look up.

No words, and yet a voice that reaches everywhere. That's the puzzle at the center of a short psalm, the nineteenth in the Bible's book of Psalms. Its writer looks up, and what comes out isn't a description of the sky. It's a claim that the sky is talking: not in Hebrew, not in any language, and never silent. It belongs to the Jewish and Christian scriptures, and some readers from other homes keep its first line for their own looking. On the thousandth day of this path, here it is.
screen: `NO WORDS, YET A VOICE.` → `THE SKY IS TALKING.` → `PSALM 19.`

segments.voice: First, the opening line, in the King James words: "The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork." Declare is a strong verb. The sky isn't just pretty; it's telling something, the way a messenger tells news. Second, the rhythm: "Day unto day uttereth speech, and night unto night sheweth knowledge." Each day hands the message to the next, each night to the next night, like a relay that has never stopped. You didn't miss the start; it's still going. Third, the riddle. The King James reads: "There is no speech nor language, where their voice is not heard." Some readers hear the Hebrew differently: there is no speech, there are no words, their voice is not heard. And yet, the next verse says, it goes out through all the earth. A speech made of no words at all. Maybe that's why it reaches everyone: nobody needs a translation. Fourth, the turn. Halfway through, the psalm moves from the sky to the teaching: "The law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul". The same writer reads two books, the heavens above and the words in hand, and finds them saying something alike. For someone on this path, of any faith or none, the first book is open every evening. You don't have to agree with what it says to stand still and listen.
screen: `THE SKY IS TELLING SOMETHING.` · `DAY UNTO DAY, NIGHT UNTO NIGHT.` · `A SPEECH WITH NO WORDS.` · `TWO BOOKS: SKY AND TEACHING.` · then, large: `THE HEAVENS DECLARE.`

segments.voice: Look at the sky now, through a window or outside, whatever's there: the blue or the gray, a star, a plane, the town's glow on the clouds. Listen with your eyes, the way you'd listen to someone speaking a language you don't know: not the words, the tone. If you pray, you can say the psalm's first line quietly and leave the rest to the sky.
Firmament. The sky itself, which the psalm says shows God's handiwork and speaks, day to day and night to night, with no words. Today's word.
Your line: day unto day uttereth speech. The relay has been running the whole time, every evening and every dawn. That's day one thousand.

1001.title: Consider the lilies
1001.hook: Solomon in all his glory wasn't dressed like one of these (Matthew 6:28–29)
1001.howItsDone: Christians read this passage from the Sermon on the Mount as a teaching on trust in God's care; some people on other paths use it as a prompt to spend a few minutes studying one plant or flower closely.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was firmament, the sky that speaks with no words. Your line was day unto day uttereth speech.

Most feet step right over it: a weed growing out of a crack in the sidewalk, with one yellow flower. Nobody planted it. Nobody waters it. Everyone's on the way to somewhere important. In the Sermon on the Mount, Matthew's Gospel has Jesus point his listeners at exactly this kind of thing: not a temple, not a sunset, but wildflowers in a field. And he sets them beside a king: Solomon, in all his glory. The flowers, he says, win.
screen: `A WEED IN A CRACK.` → `WILDFLOWERS IN A FIELD.` → `THE FLOWERS WIN.`

segments.voice: First, the instruction. In the King James words: "Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin". Consider is the verb. Not glance at, not admire in passing: look long enough to see how they grow. Second, the comparison: "And yet I say unto you, That even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these." All that wealth, all that work, and a flower that did nothing outdressed it. Awe here doesn't come from size. It comes from looking closely at something ordinary until it stops being ordinary. Third, the setting. The lilies sit inside a passage about worry. Just before them come the birds: "they sow not, neither do they reap, nor gather into barns; yet your heavenly Father feedeth them." Just after, the grass of the field, "which to day is, and to morrow is cast into the oven". The flowers don't last. That's part of the point: something that won't be here next week is still dressed with care today. Fourth, where it lands: "Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself." In the passage, take no thought is about worry, not about planning. For Christians, the lilies point to God's care. For anyone, they offer a small door out of tomorrow's list and into this one living thing, right now.
screen: `CONSIDER: LOOK LONG ENOUGH.` · `MORE THAN SOLOMON'S GLORY.` · `HERE TODAY, GONE TOMORROW.` · `NO THOUGHT FOR THE MORROW.` · then, large: `CONSIDER THE LILIES.`

segments.voice: Find one flower, a houseplant, a weed, a bouquet, or a leaf or a photo if that's what's near, and look at it as if you had to describe it to someone who's never seen one: the color at the center, the shape of each petal, where the stem bends. When your mind slips to tomorrow's list, come back to the flower. If you pray, the looking can become thanks.
Solomon. The king in all his glory, whom Jesus said was not arrayed like a single wildflower that does no work. Today's word.
Your line: dressed better than a king. Solomon had all his glory, and a wildflower still outdressed him. See you tomorrow.
